items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (Despite being composed ...), mid-sentence blank; the poem, named in a possessive phrase, is the right subject and the poet introduced in sentence 1 heads the hardest foil
items.passage: In 1854, French poet Frédéric Mistral cofounded an association dedicated to restoring the traditional language of southern France as a literary medium. Despite being composed in Provençal rather than in standard French, ______ inspiring an 1864 opera by Charles Gounod and contributing to Mistral’s 1904 Nobel Prize in Literature.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Mistral’s 1859 epic poem Mirèio found admirers across Europe,
Mistral found admirers across Europe for his 1859 epic poem Mirèio,
there were admirers across Europe for Mistral’s 1859 epic poem Mirèio,
the admirers of Mistral’s 1859 epic poem Mirèio came from across Europe,
items.explanation: The phrase “Despite being composed in Provençal rather than in standard French” describes a piece of writing, so the noun right after the comma must name that piece of writing. Choice A places “Mistral’s 1859 epic poem Mirèio” immediately after the phrase, making clear that the poem, not the poet or anyone else, was composed in Provençal.

B.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the poet introduced in sentence 1
B.why_wrong: Placing “Mistral” immediately after the phrase illogically suggests that Mistral himself was composed in Provençal.

C.why_wrong: Placing “there” immediately after the phrase leaves the phrase with no noun that it can logically describe, so the modifier dangles.

D.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the admirers
D.why_wrong: Placing “the admirers” immediately after the phrase illogically suggests that the admirers were composed in Provençal.

items.notes: Subject: Frédéric Mistral’s Provençal epic Mirèio (literature). Real subject known well; facts kept to the settled ones (Félibrige cofounded 1854, Mirèio 1859, Gounod’s opera Mireille 1864, 1904 Nobel Prize). No invented names. Band 7 as 37e5c794 (opener describes a thing; foils E, W, W): the key opens with a possessive (“Mistral’s ...”), a form students learn to distrust, while the hardest foil starts with the poet named in sentence 1; 16 run words after the blank. Every option is grammatical on its own; only the subject differs.

review.note: key was visible in the file-schema dump before the blind solve; solved the same way regardless

band7.why: Mirrors 37e5c794: a Despite + being opener describing a thing, foils W (the poet from sentence 1), E and W (the admirers); the key opens with a possessive (“Mistral’s ...”) whose head is the poem, so the student must find the head noun rather than reject possessives; 16 run words after the blank.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: -ing participial opener, passage-final blank; the animal is the right subject, foils start with its tongue, its possessive and an expletive
items.passage: The honey possum, a mouse-sized marsupial, is found only in the heathlands and coastal woodlands of southwestern Australia. Feeding almost exclusively on the nectar and pollen of flowering plants such as banksias, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: a long, brush-tipped tongue lets the honey possum reach deep inside each flower.
the honey possum’s long, brush-tipped tongue can reach deep inside each flower.
the honey possum uses its long, brush-tipped tongue to reach deep inside each flower.
there is a long, brush-tipped tongue that the honey possum uses to reach deep inside each flower.
items.explanation: The phrase “Feeding almost exclusively on the nectar and pollen of flowering plants such as banksias” describes the honey possum. Choice C places “the honey possum” immediately after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the animal, not its tongue, is the one feeding on nectar and pollen.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the tongue
A.why_wrong: Placing “a long, brush-tipped tongue” immediately after the phrase illogically suggests that the tongue itself feeds on nectar and pollen.

B.why_wrong: The subject is “the honey possum’s long, brush-tipped tongue,” not the honey possum, so the sentence illogically says that the tongue feeds on nectar and pollen.

D.why_wrong: Placing “there” immediately after the phrase leaves the phrase with no noun that it can logically describe, so the modifier dangles.

items.notes: Subject: the honey possum (Tarsipes rostratus), a nectar- and pollen-feeding marsupial of southwestern Australia (science, zoology). Real animal; facts are standard (mouse-sized, nectar and pollen diet, brush-tipped tongue, banksias). Band 6 as 9df6da04 and dab8b8ee: plain right subject after an -ing opener, passage-final full-clause options; foils W, P, E. Key neither the longest nor the shortest option.

band7.why: Matches its band-6 models 9df6da04 and dab8b8ee: plain right subject after an -ing opener, passage-final full-clause options, foils W, P and E.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: past participial opener “Compared with that of ...”, mid-sentence blank; the right subject is a property (the range of a piano), not the piano
items.passage: A modern concert grand piano has 88 keys, which collectively span slightly more than seven octaves. Compared with that of a modern grand, ______ fortepianos manufactured in Vienna in the 1780s, for instance, typically had keyboards spanning only about five octaves.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: an eighteenth-century piano had a far narrower range:
the range of an eighteenth-century piano was far narrower:
there was a far narrower range on an eighteenth-century piano:
an eighteenth-century piano was far more limited in range:
items.explanation: In the phrase “Compared with that of a modern grand,” the word “that” stands for something belonging to a modern grand piano: its range. Choice B places “the range of an eighteenth-century piano” immediately after the phrase, so the sentence logically compares one piano’s range with another’s.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the piano itself
A.why_wrong: Placing “an eighteenth-century piano” immediately after the phrase illogically compares a whole piano with the range of a modern grand.

C.why_wrong: Placing “there” immediately after the phrase leaves the comparison with no noun to attach to, so the modifier dangles.

D.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the piano itself, second predicate
D.why_wrong: Placing “an eighteenth-century piano” immediately after the phrase illogically compares the piano itself, rather than its range, with the range of a modern grand.

items.notes: Subject: keyboard range of 1780s Viennese fortepianos against a modern grand (arts, music history). General, well-established facts (modern grand 88 keys, about 7 1/3 octaves; Viennese fortepianos of the 1780s about five octaves); no named makers or composers, to avoid a famous name. Band 7 as 2dd1b8bf and fced396a: the right subject is a property (“the range of”), and the hardest foil starts with the obvious noun (the piano); foils W, E, W. 17 run words after the blank. Review: D (composers) was a one-glance reject; it now starts with the obvious noun, as two foils do in 2dd1b8bf.

fixes: replaced D (eighteenth-century composers, a one-glance reject) with a second foil built on the obvious noun, “an eighteenth-century piano was far more limited in range:”, as 2dd1b8bf has two; all four options retested in the full sentence, only B grammatical

band7.why: As 2dd1b8bf and fced396a: “Compared with that of” makes the right subject a property (“the range of”), two foils now start with the obvious noun (the piano) with different predicates, plus an expletive; 17 run words after the blank.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: noun-phrase appositive opener, mid-sentence blank; the painting, named by its title, is the right subject and the painter heads a foil
items.passage: Biographical information about the Chinese painter Wang Ximeng is scarce, and only a single painting attributed to him survives. A silk handscroll nearly twelve meters long, ______ depicts mountains, rivers, villages, and bridges in brilliant blues and greens derived from powdered minerals.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Wang Ximeng completed A Thousand Li of Rivers and Mountains in 1113, a painting that
the year 1113 saw the completion of Wang Ximeng’s A Thousand Li of Rivers and Mountains, which
it was in 1113 that Wang Ximeng completed A Thousand Li of Rivers and Mountains, which
A Thousand Li of Rivers and Mountains, which Wang Ximeng completed in 1113,
items.explanation: The phrase “A silk handscroll nearly twelve meters long” describes the painting. Choice D places the painting’s title, “A Thousand Li of Rivers and Mountains,” immediately after the phrase, so the sentence clearly identifies the painting as the handscroll.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the painter
A.why_wrong: Placing “Wang Ximeng” immediately after the phrase illogically suggests that the painter was a silk handscroll.

B.recipe: nominalised version with the wrong subject (N): the year
B.why_wrong: Placing “the year 1113” immediately after the phrase illogically suggests that a year was a silk handscroll.

C.why_wrong: Placing “it” immediately after the phrase leaves the phrase with no noun that it can logically describe, so the modifier dangles.

items.notes: Subject: Wang Ximeng’s A Thousand Li of Rivers and Mountains (arts, Chinese painting). Real work known well: silk handscroll about 11.9 m long, dated 1113, blue-green mineral pigments, the painter’s only surviving work, little known about his life. Band 6 as 5b8f9cf2: appositive opener, blank mid-sentence, the key is the work’s title plus a relative clause; foils W (painter), N (the year), E. Key is the shortest option.

band7.why: R3_appositive has no band-7 official items (appendix of spec/rw/band7/form_structure_and_sense.md), so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 like 5b8f9cf2 (title-plus-relative-clause key, painter and year foils).

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: individual possession of two nouns, with “each metal’s” after the blank as the cue
items.passage: Brass, an alloy of copper and zinc, has been manufactured since antiquity, yet early metalworkers could not produce it by simply combining the two metals in molten form. The obstacle was that ______ melting points differ substantially, with each metal’s lying hundreds of degrees away from the other’s: zinc melts at roughly 420°C and vaporizes at 907°C, whereas copper remains solid until 1,085°C.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The text refers to two separate melting points, as “each metal’s” and “the other’s” make clear, so each noun needs its own singular possessive: “copper’s and zinc’s.” Both apostrophes show that one melting point belongs to copper and another belongs to zinc.

A.why_wrong: The context requires the singular possessive nouns “copper’s” and “zinc’s,” not the plural nouns “coppers” and “zincs.”

C.recipe: plural noun where a possessive is needed (first slot)
C.why_wrong: The context requires the singular possessive noun “copper’s,” not the plural noun “coppers.”

D.recipe: joint possession for separately owned things
D.why_wrong: Marking only “zinc’s” suggests a single set of melting points shared by copper and zinc together, but the text says that “each metal’s” melting point lies far from “the other’s.”

items.notes: Subject: why early brass was hard to make (science, metallurgy and history of technology). Standard values: zinc melts at 420°C and boils at 907°C, copper melts at 1,085°C; the colon gives both melting points and zinc’s boiling point, which is why melting the two together failed. Band 7 as 4c335aea (same four-cell grid: plural-plural, possessive-possessive, plural-possessive, joint): the cue for individual possession, “each metal’s ... the other’s,” sits after the blank, as “each genre’s” does in the model. The key is the longest option by one or two characters, as in the model (an apostrophe grid key carries the extra marks).

fixes: cue reworded from “each metal’s falling hundreds of degrees from the other’s” (read as a melting point dropping) to “each metal’s lying hundreds of degrees away from the other’s”; D why_wrong updated to match

band7.why: Same four-cell grid as 4c335aea (plural-plural, possessive-possessive, plural-possessive, joint possession), with the individual-possession cue (“each metal’s ... the other’s”) after the blank, as “each genre’s” is in the model.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: missing main verb after a dash-enclosed description that holds its own finite verbs
items.passage: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter—a tenth-century narrative in which an elderly woodcutter discovers a tiny girl inside a luminous bamboo stalk and raises her as his daughter until she must return to the Moon—______ a distinguished position in Japanese literature as the earliest surviving prose narrative in the language.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence’s subject is “The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter,” and the description between the dashes does not supply its verb. The sentence needs a finite main verb after the second dash, and the present tense verb “holds” provides it.

B.recipe: nonfinite (-ing) where a finite verb is needed
B.why_wrong: The nonfinite participle “holding” leaves the sentence without a finite main verb, so the sentence is incomplete.

C.recipe: nonfinite (to + base) where a finite verb is needed
C.why_wrong: The nonfinite to-infinitive “to hold” leaves the sentence without a finite main verb, so the sentence is incomplete.

D.recipe: nonfinite (having + past participle) where a finite verb is needed
D.why_wrong: The nonfinite perfect participle “having held” leaves the sentence without a finite main verb, so the sentence is incomplete.

items.notes: Subject: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter (Taketori Monogatari) (literature). Real work known well: tenth century, a girl found in a shining bamboo stalk, raised by the old woodcutter, who at last returns to the Moon; usually called the oldest surviving Japanese prose narrative. Band 6 as a75d5984: subject head 33 words from the blank behind a dash pair whose own verbs (discovers, raises) read like the main verb; canonical option set {finite, -ing, to + base, having + participle}.

band7.why: R2_finite_main has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 as a75d5984: the subject head sits 33 words before the blank behind a dash pair holding its own finite verbs.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: absolute phrase (complete clause, comma, possessive noun, blank); every finite foil would make a comma splice
items.passage: Most orchids photosynthesize through their leaves. The ghost orchid, a rare epiphyte native to the subtropical swamps of southern Florida and western Cuba, lacks leaves entirely, its flattened green roots ______ photosynthesis while anchoring the plant to the trunks of host trees such as pond apple and bald cypress.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The text before the second comma is already a complete main clause (the subject “The ghost orchid” with the finite verb “lacks”). What follows must be a supplementary phrase rather than a second clause, and the nonfinite participle “conducting” forms that phrase, describing what the orchid’s roots do.

A.recipe: finite (present) where a nonfinite is needed: comma splice
A.why_wrong: With the finite verb “conduct,” the words after the second comma form an independent clause joined to the first one with only a comma, which is a comma splice.

B.recipe: finite (present progressive) where a nonfinite is needed: comma splice
B.why_wrong: With the finite verb “are conducting,” the words after the comma form a second independent clause joined to the first with only a comma, which is a comma splice.

C.recipe: finite (present perfect) where a nonfinite is needed: comma splice
C.why_wrong: With the finite verb “have conducted,” the words after the comma form a second independent clause joined to the first with only a comma, which is a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: the ghost orchid (Dendrophylax lindenii), leafless, photosynthesizing through its roots (science, botany). Real plant known well (Florida and Cuba swamps, an epiphyte with no leaves, green photosynthetic roots on pond apple and bald cypress). Band 7 as 81f09e07 and c88ba1b7: complete clause + comma + possessive noun + blank + object; each finite foil agrees with the plural “roots,” so each reads as a sensible clause and the error is a comma splice; 18 run words after the blank.

band7.why: As 81f09e07 and c88ba1b7: complete clause, comma, possessive noun, blank; every finite foil agrees with “roots” and makes a sensible comma splice; 17 run words after the blank.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: object pronoun for a singular noun, with plural rival nouns (“students,” “adults”) just before the blank
items.passage: Adam Mickiewicz’s Pan Tadeusz (1834), an epic poem about two feuding noble families in Lithuania in 1811 and 1812, remains a fixture of the school curriculum across Poland. Generations of Polish students have memorized its opening invocation, and many adults can still recite ______ decades after graduating.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to “its opening invocation,” a singular noun phrase, so the singular pronoun “it” is needed: many adults can still recite the invocation decades after graduating.

A.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “them” doesn’t agree in number with the singular antecedent “its opening invocation.”

B.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “those” doesn’t agree in number with the singular antecedent “its opening invocation.”

D.why_wrong: The pronoun “one” would refer to some unspecified example rather than to the invocation already mentioned, so the sentence no longer says what the adults can recite.

items.notes: Subject: Mickiewicz’s Pan Tadeusz and its memorized opening invocation (literature). Real work known well (1834, set in Lithuania in 1811 and 1812, two feuding gentry families, required school reading in Poland). Medium as 2.15 and 2.3: the antecedent sits in the same sentence but plural nouns (“Generations,” “students,” “adults”) come between it and the blank.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head (“craft”) behind a participial phrase with plural nouns (lexical-verb options)
items.passage: Chikankari is a style of white-on-white embroidery that has been associated with the northern Indian city of Lucknow for centuries. The craft, practiced today predominantly by women artisans working from their homes throughout the surrounding region, ______ on approximately three dozen distinct stitches, each with its own traditional name.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the singular noun “craft”; the phrase “practiced today predominantly by women artisans working from their homes throughout the surrounding region” only describes it. The singular verb “relies” agrees with “craft.”

A.why_wrong: The plural verb “rely” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “craft.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “are relying” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “craft.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “have relied” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “craft.”

items.notes: Subject: chikankari embroidery of Lucknow (arts, textiles). Real craft known well (white thread on fine white cloth, home-based women embroiderers, about 32 to 40 named stitches). Medium as 2.20: singular head followed by a participial phrase holding plural nouns (artisans, homes); 15 words between head and blank.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head (“map”) behind a participial phrase listing plural nouns (be-family options)
items.passage: The Hereford Mappa Mundi, drawn on a single sheet of calfskin around 1300, places Jerusalem at the center of the known world. The map, crowded with illustrations of cities, rivers, animals, biblical episodes, and mythological creatures, ______ the largest medieval map still in existence.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the singular noun “map”; the plural nouns in the phrase “crowded with illustrations of cities, rivers, animals, biblical episodes, and mythological creatures” don’t change it. The singular verb “is” agrees with “map.”

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “are” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “map.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “have been” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “map.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “were” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “map.”

items.notes: Subject: the Hereford Mappa Mundi (history, cartography). Real object known well (single sheet of vellum, about 1300, Jerusalem at the center, Hereford Cathedral calls it the largest medieval map known to still exist). A cross-text claim on mappae mundi was withdrawn in claims.txt and no live item uses it. Medium as 2.16 and 2.21: singular head behind a phrase listing five plural nouns.

review.note: no live item uses the Hereford Mappa Mundi; the cross-text mappae mundi claim (claims.txt line 139) was withdrawn at line 309

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: quantifier subject “Each of these coins” followed by a relative clause with its own plural verb
items.passage: The euro, the currency shared by numerous European countries, is issued in eight coin denominations ranging from 1 cent to 2 euros. Each of these coins, which are produced by national mints throughout the eurozone, ______ a common side whose design is identical everywhere and a national side whose design is determined by the issuing country.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is “Each,” which means each one of the coins and is singular. The phrase “of these coins” and the clause “which are produced by national mints throughout the eurozone” come between the subject and the verb but don’t change its number, so the singular verb “features” is needed.

A.why_wrong: The plural verb “feature” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “Each.”

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “are featuring” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “Each.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “have featured” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “Each.”

items.notes: Subject: euro coins, common side and national side (social science, economics). Real facts known well (eight denominations from 1 cent to 2 euros, minted by national mints, one common side and one national side); the number of member countries is left out on purpose because it changes. Medium as 2.23 (“Every last second of ..., which ...”): quantifier head followed by “of” + plural and a which-clause whose own verb is plural.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: possessive determiner (their vs its and contractions), plural antecedent before the pronoun and a singular noun (“web”) between them
items.passage: Blanket octopuses show one of the most extreme size differences between the sexes of any animal: females can grow to about two meters long, while males rarely exceed a few centimeters. When threatened, females unfurl a long, translucent web of skin stretched between ______ arms, a display that may startle predators.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The possessive determiner refers to “females,” the plural subject of the sentence, so the plural possessive “their” is needed: the web is stretched between the females’ arms.

A.why_wrong: “It’s” is a contraction of “it is” or “it has,” not a possessive, and it is singular, so it doesn’t agree with the plural antecedent “females.”

B.why_wrong: “They’re” is a contraction of “they are,” not a possessive determiner, so it can’t show that the arms belong to the females.

D.why_wrong: The singular possessive “its” doesn’t agree in number with the plural antecedent “females”; the singular nouns near the blank, “web” and “skin,” have no arms.

items.notes: Subject: the blanket octopus (Tremoctopus) female’s web display and extreme size dimorphism (science, zoology). Real animal known well (females up to about two meters, males a few centimeters, webbing between the arms unfurled when threatened). Medium: antecedent before the pronoun, one singular attractor (“web”), the 2 x 2 grid its/their by possessive/contraction.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: subject pronoun for a singular noun, no rival antecedent
items.passage: The tagua palm, a slow-growing species with a short, stout trunk, thrives in the humid rainforests of Ecuador, Colombia, and Peru. The palm’s seed is so hard and white that ______ can be carved and polished much like elephant ivory, a resemblance reflected in the nickname “vegetable ivory.”
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to “The palm’s seed,” a singular noun phrase, so the singular pronoun “it” is needed: the seed can be carved and polished much like elephant ivory.

A.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “they” doesn’t agree in number with the singular antecedent “The palm’s seed.”

C.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “these” doesn’t agree in number with the singular antecedent “The palm’s seed.”

D.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “those” doesn’t agree in number with the singular antecedent “The palm’s seed.”

items.notes: Subject: tagua palm seeds, known as vegetable ivory (science, botany). Real plant known well (Ecuador, Colombia, Peru; hard white endosperm carved like ivory). Easy as 1.39 and 1.19: the antecedent is the subject of the same sentence and there is no rival singular noun; options mix one personal pronoun of each number with demonstratives.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: object pronoun for a plural noun after “More than a thousand of”
items.passage: Between 1422 and 1509, members of the Paston family of Norfolk, England, exchanged a remarkable number of letters discussing property disputes, marriages, illnesses, and household management. More than a thousand of ______ survive, offering historians an unusually detailed view of everyday life in fifteenth-century England.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to “letters,” a plural noun, so the plural pronoun “them” is needed: more than a thousand of the letters survive.

A.why_wrong: The singular pronoun “it” doesn’t agree in number with the plural antecedent “letters.”

B.why_wrong: The singular pronoun “this” doesn’t agree in number with the plural antecedent “letters.”

C.why_wrong: The singular pronoun “that” doesn’t agree in number with the plural antecedent “letters.”

items.notes: Subject: the Paston Letters, fifteenth-century family correspondence from Norfolk (history). Real collection known well (1422 to 1509, over a thousand letters and papers, household, legal and marriage matters). Easy as 1.12: plural antecedent in the previous sentence, singular pronoun and demonstratives as foils. The key ties “this” and “that” for length (four letters), as many official pronoun keys do.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular subject right before the blank inside a that-clause (be-family options)
items.passage: With its long tail, sharp retractable claws, and catlike face, the fossa, the largest carnivore native to Madagascar, closely resembles a small cougar. Genetic evidence demonstrates, however, that the animal ______ more closely related to mongooses than to cats.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the clause is the singular noun “animal,” which refers to the fossa, so it takes the singular verb “is.”

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “are” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “animal.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “were” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “animal.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “have been” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “animal.”

items.notes: Subject: the fossa of Madagascar, catlike but closer to mongooses (science, zoology). Real animal known well (largest native carnivore of Madagascar, family Eupleridae, sister group of the mongooses). Easy as 1.40 and 1.4: singular subject directly before the blank, no number clash.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular subject right before the blank (lexical-verb options)
items.passage: A furoshiki is a square of cloth that people in Japan have used for centuries to wrap and transport everyday goods. Folded and knotted in different configurations, a single furoshiki ______ items as varied as bottles, books, and boxed lunches.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the singular noun phrase “a single furoshiki,” so it takes the singular verb “wraps.”

A.why_wrong: The plural verb “wrap” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “a single furoshiki.”

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “are wrapping” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “a single furoshiki.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “have wrapped” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “a single furoshiki.”

items.notes: Subject: the furoshiki wrapping cloth (social science, everyday culture). Real object known well; the article “a single” fixes the number (Japanese nouns have no plural form). Easy as 1.20: subject right before the blank behind a short opener, no number clash.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular subject right before the blank (lexical-verb options)
items.passage: The markhor, Pakistan’s national animal, is a wild goat that inhabits rocky mountain slopes across Central and South Asia. The male markhor ______ spectacular spiraling horns that twist like corkscrews and can reach more than a meter and a half in length.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the singular noun phrase “The male markhor,” so it takes the singular verb “grows.”

A.why_wrong: The plural verb “grow” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “The male markhor.”

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “are growing” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “The male markhor.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “have grown” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “The male markhor.”

items.notes: Subject: the markhor and its corkscrew horns (science, zoology). Real animal known well (national animal of Pakistan, male horns up to about 160 cm, checked on the Wikipedia article). Easy as 1.6: subject directly before the blank, no intervener.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: missing main verb after an appositive
items.passage: Scholars’ knowledge of early Irish storytelling derives largely from manuscripts copied by monks during the medieval period. The Táin Bó Cúailnge, the most celebrated of these tales, ______ of a war that Queen Medb of Connacht wages to capture a prized brown bull from the neighboring province of Ulster.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence’s subject is “The Táin Bó Cúailnge,” and the phrase “the most celebrated of these tales” only renames it. The sentence still needs a finite main verb, and the present tense verb “tells” supplies one.

A.recipe: nonfinite (-ing) where a finite verb is needed
A.why_wrong: The nonfinite participle “telling” leaves the sentence without a finite main verb.

C.recipe: nonfinite (to + base) where a finite verb is needed
C.why_wrong: The nonfinite to-infinitive “to tell” leaves the sentence without a finite main verb.

D.recipe: nonfinite (having + past participle) where a finite verb is needed
D.why_wrong: The nonfinite perfect participle “having told” leaves the sentence without a finite main verb.

items.notes: Subject: the Táin Bó Cúailnge, Queen Medb and the Brown Bull of Cooley (literature). Real work known well (preserved in medieval manuscripts, Medb of Connacht raids Ulster for the bull). Easy as 1.21 and 1.30: main verb missing after a short appositive; canonical option set.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: missing main verb after an introductory phrase
items.passage: Basket stars, relatives of starfish, have five arms that divide repeatedly into a tangle of thin, curling branches. At night, these animals ______ their branches into the current to capture drifting zooplankton, which they then transfer to the mouth.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence’s subject is “these animals,” and the sentence needs a finite main verb to say what they do. The present tense verb “extend” supplies it.

B.recipe: nonfinite (-ing) where a finite verb is needed
B.why_wrong: The nonfinite participle “extending” leaves the sentence without a finite main verb.

C.recipe: nonfinite (to + base) where a finite verb is needed
C.why_wrong: The nonfinite to-infinitive “to extend” leaves the sentence without a finite main verb.

D.recipe: nonfinite (having + past participle) where a finite verb is needed
D.why_wrong: The nonfinite perfect participle “having extended” leaves the sentence without a finite main verb.

items.notes: Subject: basket stars (Gorgonocephalidae), branching arms and night feeding (science, marine biology). Real animals known well. Easy as 1.23 and 1.31: bare main-verb slot after a short subject; canonical option set.

items.subtype: Tense: simple present for a habitual action, parallel with a present verb in the previous sentence
items.passage: Dugongs, large marine mammals inhabiting warm coastal waters from East Africa to Australia, feed almost exclusively on seagrass. While grazing, a dugong ______ entire plants from the seafloor, roots included, leaving behind meandering trails of exposed sediment that researchers use to map where the animals have fed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The text describes what dugongs regularly do, and the first sentence uses the present tense (“feed”) for that habit. The simple present “pulls” continues this description of habitual behavior.

A.recipe: past perfect where the cue is present
A.why_wrong: The past perfect “had pulled” describes an action completed before another past action, but the text describes something dugongs habitually do.

B.recipe: simple past where present is needed
B.why_wrong: The simple past “pulled” describes a completed action in the past, but the text describes a present-day habit.

D.why_wrong: The future perfect “will have pulled” describes an action that will be completed by some future time, which doesn’t fit a description of habitual behavior.

items.notes: Subject: dugongs uprooting seagrass and leaving feeding trails (science, marine biology). Real animal known well (seagrass diet, whole plants uprooted, feeding trails surveyed by researchers). Easy as 1.17 and 1.37: present habitual cue (“feed,” “While grazing”); foils past perfect, simple past, future perfect (no progressive beside the habitual cue, no present perfect).

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: two-slot grid (singular possessor + plural noun)
items.passage: The kapok tree, which can exceed 60 meters in height, is native to the tropical Americas and to West Africa. When ripe, the ______ split open to release seeds embedded in a fluffy, water-resistant fiber that manufacturers once used extensively as stuffing for life jackets and mattresses.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The singular possessive “tree’s” shows that the seed pods belong to the kapok tree, and the plural noun “pods” shows that there is more than one pod (the plural verb “split” confirms this). Nothing belongs to the pods, so “pods” takes no apostrophe.

A.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
A.why_wrong: The context requires the plural noun “pods,” not the singular possessive noun “pod’s”; nothing belongs to the pods.

B.why_wrong: The context requires the singular possessive noun “tree’s,” not the plural noun “trees”; the pods belong to the kapok tree.

C.why_wrong: The context requires the singular possessive “tree’s” and the plural “pods,” not the plural “trees” and the singular possessive “pod’s.”

items.notes: Subject: kapok tree seed pods and kapok fiber (science, botany). Real tree known well (up to 60 to 70 m, native to the tropical Americas and West Africa, buoyant water-resistant fiber used in life jackets and mattresses). Easy as 1.16: two-slot grid, singular possessor + plural noun; number cues “The kapok tree” and the plural verb “split.”

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: purpose to-infinitive after a complete clause
items.passage: British nurse Kate Marsden was among the first women elected to the Royal Geographical Society. In 1891, she journeyed thousands of kilometers across Siberia, much of the way on horseback, ______ an herb reputed to alleviate the symptoms of leprosy.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “she journeyed thousands of kilometers across Siberia” is already complete. The to-infinitive “to find” correctly begins a phrase that gives the purpose of her journey.

A.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
A.why_wrong: The finite verb “finds” can’t follow the complete clause as a second main verb without a conjunction, and its present tense doesn’t fit an 1891 journey.

C.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
C.why_wrong: The finite verb “found” can’t follow the complete clause as a second main verb without a conjunction such as “and.”

D.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
D.why_wrong: The finite verb “has found” can’t follow the complete clause as a second main verb without a conjunction.

items.notes: Subject: Kate Marsden’s 1891 Siberian journey in search of a leprosy remedy (history). Real person known well (one of the first women fellows of the Royal Geographical Society, 1892; traveled to Yakutia seeking an herb rumored to help leprosy). Easy as 1.22: purpose infinitive after a complete clause; foils V-s, V-ed, has V-ed.

items.subtype: Tense: past perfect for an action earlier than a stated past time (the 1870s)
items.passage: In the 1870s, American inventor Thomas Adams began commercially producing chewing gum from chicle, the dried sap of the sapodilla tree, which is native to southern Mexico and Central America. Chicle was hardly a novelty, however: the Maya ______ it for centuries before Adams’s product appeared in stores.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The text says the Maya chewed chicle “for centuries before Adams’s product appeared in stores,” which happened in the 1870s. The past perfect “had chewed” shows that this action took place before that past event.

B.why_wrong: The future tense “will chew” doesn’t fit an action that took place before the 1870s.

C.recipe: present progressive where past perfect is needed
C.why_wrong: The present progressive “are chewing” describes an action happening now, not one completed before Adams’s product appeared in stores.

D.recipe: present simple where past perfect is needed
D.why_wrong: The present tense “chew” doesn’t fit an action that took place before a past event in the 1870s.

items.notes: Subject: chicle chewing gum, Thomas Adams, and earlier Maya use (history, with botany). Real facts known well (Adams began making chicle gum in the early 1870s; chicle from Manilkara zapota; the Maya chewed it long before). Easy as 1.24: earlier-than-past action with an explicit cue (“for centuries before ... appeared”).

items.subtype: Tense: simple past for a completed action tied to a past date
items.passage: The Great Stalacpipe Organ in Virginia’s Luray Caverns produces music by tapping ancient stalactites with rubber-tipped mallets. Before the instrument was completed in 1956, its designer, Leland Sprinkle, ______ three years searching the caverns for stalactites that produced the right notes.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The text says the instrument “was completed in 1956,” and Sprinkle’s search came before that, so the action is in the past. The simple past “spent” correctly describes this completed action.

A.recipe: present simple where the cue is a past date
A.why_wrong: The present tense “spends” doesn’t fit an action completed before 1956.

B.why_wrong: The future tense “will spend” doesn’t fit an action completed before 1956.

D.recipe: present progressive where the cue is a past date
D.why_wrong: The present progressive “is spending” describes an action happening now, not one completed before 1956.

items.notes: Subject: the Great Stalacpipe Organ in Luray Caverns and its designer Leland W. Sprinkle (arts, music and technology history). Facts checked on the Wikipedia article (rubber mallets tap stalactites; designed and built by Sprinkle over three years, completed 1956). Easy as 1.13 and 1.32: dated past cue in the same sentence; foils present, future, present progressive (no present perfect beside the date).
